html:
The Hundred Years' War was a long series of wars between the kings of England and France, from 1337 to 1453, fought over English lands in France and over the French crown itself.

Its roots lay in the Norman conquest of 1066, which made the kings of England also great lords in France. By the 1300s they held Gascony, in the south-west, as vassals of the French king, which caused endless disputes. In 1337 the French king Philip VI seized Gascony, and Edward III of England, whose mother was a French princess, claimed the throne of France.

It had three main phases, broken by truces, plague and civil wars:

  • 1337 to 1360: English archers with longbows won great victories at Crécy in 1346 and Poitiers in 1356, where they captured the French king. England took Calais. The Black Death struck in the middle of it.
  • 1369 to 1389: France won back most of the lost land.
  • 1415 to 1453: Henry V won at Agincourt in 1415 and, allied with Burgundy, conquered northern France. Then Joan of Arc raised the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned. French cannon drove the English out, and the fall of Bordeaux in 1453 ended the war.

England kept only Calais, lost in 1558. The lands of the English crown became an island kingdom. France came out with a stronger king, a standing army and a sense of nation. Side wars, such as the succession war in Brittany, were pulled in.
sum: The Hundred Years' War was a long series of wars between the kings of England and France, from 1337 to 1453, fought over English lands in France and over the French crown itself.
